# Abstract

## Aims

To estimate national age-specific, sex-specific, and age-standardized
incidence of diag-nosed diabetes in Peru from 2016 to 2023.

## Methods

We analyzed repeated cross-sectional data from the Demographic and
Family Health Sur-vey (ENDES), an annual nationally representative
household survey, estimating the preva-lence of self-reported
physician-diagnosed diabetes in adults aged 20 years and older. Smoothed
prevalence was combined with United Nations general-population mortality
and published diabetes mortality rate ratios in an illness-death model,
which recovers in-cidence from the change in prevalence with age and
calendar time. Uncertainty was propagated through 1,000 simulations.

## Results

Among 294,549 participants, 9,002 (3.1%) reported diagnosed diabetes.
Age-standardized incidence increased from 4.46 (95% CI 3.61-5.23) to
8.58 (5.27–14.41) per 1,000 person-years in men and from 5.20
(4.27–6.19) to 9.87 (6.16–16.07) in women. Corresponding IRRs were 1.93
(1.14–3.24) and 1.92 (1.15–3.16). Relative increases were greatest at
young-er ages.

## Conclusions

Diagnosed diabetes incidence in Peru approximately doubled between 2016
and 2023, with proportionally larger increases among younger adults.
These findings support strengthened diabetes prevention and surveillance
while highlighting the value of routine-ly collected survey data for
estimating incidence in settings where longitudinal cohorts are
unavailable.

## Key words

Diabetes, epidemiology, disease burden, Peru

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 1. Introduction

In 2025, the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) estimated that over
588 million people aged 20-79 years were living with diabetes
globally.[@maglianoDiabetesAtlas2025] The South and Central America
region ranked 5th out of the seven IDF regions of the world in the
prevalence of diabetes, the region has gone through a rapid
intensification of its epidemic as the age standardized prevalence of
diabetes nearly tripled between 2000 and 2024, from 3.7% to 10.1%, and
the number of adults aged 20 to 79 years living with diabetes grew from
8.6 million in 2000 to 35.4 million in 2024, and is projected to
increase to 52 million by 2050.[@maglianoDiabetesAtlas2025]

Peru is an upper middle-income economy situated in South
America,[@WorldBankGroup] the country has the 4th largest population in
the region with around 34 million people living in the country in
2025.[@censo] Over the past decades, Peru has experienced a growth in
the burden of non-communicable disease as the result of urbanization,
population ageing, and the nutritional
transition.[@villenaDiabetesMellitusPeru2015] Indeed, cardiovascular
disease and diabetes were two of the top causes of death within the
country in 2021.[@WHO_Peru_2026]

Even though Peru is one of the South American countries with the lowest
prevalence rates of diabetes in the region, these rates has been
steadily increasing since
2005,[@vera-poncePrevalenceDiabetesPrediabetes2025] and according to the
IDF Atlas, in 2024 the prevalence among adults 20-79 years was
6.0%.[@maglianoDiabetesAtlas2025] Moreover, the Global Burden of Disease
Study estimated an age standardized incidence of diabetes that increased
significantly between 1990 and 2017, with an age-standardized rate
rising from 162 per 100,000 people in 1990 to 203 per 100,000 in
2017.[@liuTrendsIncidenceDiabetes2020] It should be noted that the NCD
Risk Factor Collaboration has reported a prevalence of 17.5% for Peru
(all ages) based on a Bayesian modeling approach using data that include
HbA1c as a diagnostic criterion as well as non representative samples.
Evidence from Peru suggests a particularly high burden. The PERUDIAB
study, an urban household cohort of adults aged 25 years or older
reported a cumulative incidence of diabetes of 7.2% and an incidence
rate of 19.5 new cases per 1,000 person-years \[95% confidence interval
(95% CI) 13.9 - 28.3\]. [@seclenElevatedIncidenceRates2017]

Reports on diabetes incidence in Peru remain limited, and the few
available studies have been conducted primarily in urban populations.
Direct estimation of incidence requires data from cohort studies, which
are scarce in Peru and across Latin America. In this context an
alternative is to estimate incidence rates of diabetes based on the
mathematical relation between the age-specific prevalence of diabetes,
the mortality rate of the general population, and the mortality rate
ratio, an approach that has been validated for chronic
conditions,[@brinksAgeTimedependentModel2014] and applied to a
comparable Latin American
setting.[@silverman-retanaUsingIllnessdeathModel2024] Therefore, the
objective of this study was to estimate age-specific, sex-specific, and
age-standardized incidence rates of diabetes in Peru between 2016 and
2023 by implementing the illness–death model.

# 2. Subjects, Materials and Methods

## 2.1 Estimation of input prevalence

An observational study was conducted using cross-sectional data from the
Demographic and Family Health Surveys (ENDES) for the period 2015–2023.
The ENDES survey is conducted annually and is representative of the
Peruvian population based on a multilevel sampling
approach[@institutonacionaldeestadísticaeinformática2026]. It provides
information on demographic characteristics, health indicators across the
life course, communicable and non-communicable diseases, and related
determinants.[@EncuestaDemograficaSalud]

The target population comprises households and their resident members,
with data collected by trained personnel who visit the selected
households. The instruments for data collection include interviews and
laboratory measurements.[@EncuestaDemograficaSalud] Prevalent cases of
diabetes were identified with the questions: "Has a doctor ever
diagnosed you with diabetes or 'high sugar' in your blood?". This
question offers the response options: "yes", "no", and "don't know/don't
remember".[@EncuestaDemograficaSalud] For the analyses, only
participants who respond "yes" or "no" were included.

Age- and sex-specific prevalence estimates of diabetes were calculated
for each survey year, accounting for the complex ENDES sampling design
using primary sampling units, strata, and sampling weights. Age groups
were categorized in five-year intervals from 20 years up to 80+ years,
with 95% CI calculated using logit transformation. Because estimation of
incidence requires information on temporal changes in prevalence,
estimates from 2015 were included as model input, whereas incidence
estimates were re-ported from 2016 onwards.

## 2.2 Estimating the incidence rate of diabetes

To estimate incidence using the approach described below, information on
the mortality rate of the overall population $m$ (general mortality) and
mortality rate ratio (MRR) comparing people with and without diabetes is
required. Since no studies to date have estimated the MRR for Peru, as
in previous studies we assumed a log-linear relationship for age and MRR
between age with values ranging from 7.5–8.5 at age 30 and 2.5–3.0 at
age 80.[@silverman-retanaUsingIllnessdeathModel2024] For $m$, we used
data from the United Nations World Population
Prospects.[@worldpopulation2024] Both the ENDES survey data and the
United Nations mortality data are publicly available and can be accessed
here (https://proyectos.inei.gob.pe/endes/ and
https://population.un.org/dataportal/home?df=281d63a9-ed9a-48c1-9947-43927365464f).

To estimate the incidence rate of diabetes for the years 2016-2023, an
illness-death model was applied using a partial differential equation.
This method has previously been used in the context of chronic
non-communicable diseases.[@brinksAgeTimedependentModel2014;
@hassAgespecificIncidenceNeed2023] This model is based on a mathematical
relationship between the prevalence of diabetes, the mortality rate in
the general population, and the MRR. Transitions between these states
are characterized by incidence rates (no diabetes → diabetes) and
mortality rates (no diabetes → death; diabetes → death).

The partial differential equation used to estimate the incidence of
diabetes was developed by Brinks and
Landwehr[@brinksAgeTimedependentModel2014] and describes the change in
prevalence with respect to age and calendar time:

$$i = \frac{\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial a} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \right)p}{1 - p} + m \cdot \frac{p (MRR - 1)}{p (MRR - 1) + 1}$$

Where $i$ represents the incidence of diabetes, $p$ represents the
prevalence, and
$\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial a} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \right)p$
denotes the temporal change in prevalence as a function of age $a$ and
calendar time $t$. Therefore, the incidence rate can be calculated from
estimates of the prevalence of diabetes, its temporal change by age and
calendar time, the overall mortality rate, and the ratio of mortality
rates between individuals with and without diabetes.

To smooth the prevalence estimates from the ENDES survey, we regressed
the logit-transformed prevalence estimates on age, calender time and sex
using linear regression. We allowed for a non-linear relationship
between age and the log-odds of prevalence by including a third-degree
polynomial for age. Calendar time was included as a linear term. We used
expit-transformed predicted values from this linear regression as input
prevalence for the partial differential equation.

To account for uncertainty in the input data, we repeated the estimation
of the incidence rate 1,000 times and varied the input prevalence and
MRR. For each iteration, we sampled the MRR from a normal distribution
within the ranges described above. For age and sex-specific prevalence
estimates, we shifted the point estimates using a random draw from a
normal distribution scaled by the corresponding standard errors. From
the resulting distribution of incidence estimates, we reported the
median as point estimate and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile as
95%-confidence bounds.

All statistical analyses were performed in the R software version
4.5.0.[@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2023].

# Results

During the study period, 294,549 participants from the ENDES population
survey were included; of these, 9,002 (3.1%) reported having been
diagnosed with diabetes by their treating physician (Table 1). Figure 1
shows the prevalence of diabetes by age and sex, estimated from ENDES
data using logit-transformed prevalence estimates. These estimates were
used as input data in the illness-death model described above, along
with the general population mortality rate and the MRR, to obtain the
diabetes incidence rate for each year of analysis by sex (Figure 2) and
the age-specific rate by sex for each year of analysis (Figure 3).

Between 2016 and 2023, the age-standardized incidence rate (IR) of
diabetes showed a sustained increase in both sexes. Among men, the IR of
diabetes rose from 4.46 (95% CI: 3.61 to 5.23) per 1,000 in 2016 to 8.58
(95% CI: 5.27 to 14.41) per 1,000 in 2023, corresponding to an incidence
rate ratio (IRR) of 1.93 (95% CI: 1.14 to 3.24) compared with 2016.
Similarly, among women, the IR of diabetes increased from 5.20 (95% CI:
4.27 to 6.19) per 1,000 in 2016 to 9.87 (95% CI: 6.16 to 16.07) per
1,000 in 2023, with an IRR of 1.92 (95% CI: 1.15 to 3.16) relative to
the reference year (Table 2).

When stratified by age group and calendar period, the IR of diabetes
increased between 2016 and 2023 across all age groups in both sexes. The
older age groups exhibited the highest IRs of diabetes in the
population, reaching in 2023 an IR of diabetes of 22.54 (95% CI: 13.49
to 36.57) per 1,000 among 60-year-old men and 25.76 (95% CI: 16.10 to
43.11) per 1,000 among 60-year-old women. However, analysis of the IRR
indicated that the largest and most relevant relative increases occurred
in the younger age groups. When comparing rates of diabetes in the year
2023 with those in 2016, among 20-year-old age group, the IRR was 2.18
(95% CI: 1.00 to 4.21) in men and 2.16 (95% CI: 1.03 to 4.28) in women;
important differences were observed in the 30-year-old age group, with
IRRs of 2.13 (95% CI: 1.17 to 3.76) and 2.11 (95% CI: 1.25 to 3.52),
respectively (Table 3).

# Discussion

Our study applied the illness-death model to estimate the incidence of
diabetes in Peru by using prevalence data from nationally representative
surveys and mortality data from official vital statistics. Our findings
showed that the incidence of diabetes in Peru has been steadily
increasing in men and women since 2016, and reached its highest absolute
levels in late midlife. We observed that the relative increase in
diabetes incidence was markedly higher in the younger age groups, in
particular among men in their 20's, and women in their 20's and 30's,
suggesting a possible shift towards earlier diabetes onset.

Our estimates should be interpreted alongside, rather than as directly
comparable with, previous Peruvian cohort studies.The cumulative
incidence estimates from our study were smaller than those reported in
the PERUDIAB study,[@seclenElevatedIncidenceRates2017] but larger than
those in the CRONICAS cohort
study.[@bernabe-ortizGeographicalVariationProgression2016] These studies
estimated glycaemia defined incidence in restricted populations,
including previously undiagnosed disease, whereas our model used
self-reported physician-diagnosed diabetes from repeated national
surveys and should be interpreted as estimating diagnosed diabetes
incidence. This distinction likely contributes to the lower incidence
observed in our study.

Differences in population coverage are also relevant. PERUDIAB was an
urban cohort, while CRONICAS was based on selected sentinel sites rather
than a nationally representative
sample.[@seclenElevatedIncidenceRates2017] Additional Peruvian evidence
showed marked variation in diabetes incidence across rural,
rural-to-urban migrant, and urban populations, supporting the view that
national estimates should not be expected to reproduce rates from urban
or geographically selected
cohorts.[@bernabe-ortizGeographicalVariationProgression2016] Our
estimates of age- and sex-standardized incidence of diabetes extend
earlier findings by providing contemporary nationally representative
time series by calendar year.

Methodologically, the closest regional comparator is the study by
Silverman-Retana et al.;[@silverman-retanaUsingIllnessdeathModel2024]
their study estimated an age-standardized incidence of diabetes of 6.1
to 8.0 per 1,000 person-years in men and 6.5 to 10.6 per 1,000
person-years in women in Mexico between 2003 and 2015, with the highest
age-specific rates in the 60 to 69 year age group. Our estimates for the
Peruvian population were broadly similar in magnitude by 2023, but
increased sharply over a shorter period of time. Both studies showed
that incidence estimates peaked in later midlife. A wider comparison
with incidence rates and incidence rate trends over the past
decades,[@magliano2019] would place Peru in the middle ground among
summarized incidence rates, and in the upper range of recent incident
rate increases. The implementation of the illness-death model for
estimating nationally representative incidence rates in Latin American
contexts is a useful, and cost-effective approach where longitudinal
diabetes surveillance is limited.

The near doubling of incidence over eight years may reflect, at least in
part, changes in known upstream risk factors of type 2 diabetes in Peru.
Adiposity has increased markedly in the country: national survey
analyses indicate that the prevalence of obesity rose over the last
decade,[@vasquez-romeroPrevalenceObesityAccording2025] and that a large
share of Peruvian adults now meet criteria for preclinical or clinical
obesity.[@guerravalenciaNewDefinitionObesity2025] Because obesity
carries the highest attributable risk for diabetes in Peruvian
populations, [@bernabe-ortizGeographicalVariationProgression2016] a
rising prevalence of excess adiposity provides a plausible mechanism for
the increase in incidence we observed, alongside population ageing,
urbanisation, and the broader nutritional transition documented in
Peruvian cohorts[@carrillo-larcoTrajectoriesBodyMass2018]. We can only
speculate that obesity could be a strong driver as our model only took
age, sex, and calendar year into account. The proportionally larger
increase among younger adults aligns with international evidence that
the mean age at type 2 diabetes diagnosis is comparatively low in low-
and middle-income settings,[@lukEarlyonsetType22025] and is of
particular concern because earlier onset implies a longer lifetime
exposure to hyperglycaemia and a greater cumulative risk of
complications.[@limUnderstandingDriversConsequences2025]

The acceleration of incidence around 2020 and 2021 warrants cautious
interpretation. One contributor may be the COVID-19 pandemic: SARS-CoV-2
infection has been associated with an increased risk of new-onset
diabetes,[@xieRisksBurdensIncident2022] and the pandemic period was also
marked by weight gain, reduced physical activity, and psychosocial
stress at the population level.[@danielsSystematicReviewImpact2022
@nourEffectCOVID19Pandemic2023] At the same time, self-reported
diagnosed incidence depends on access to and use of health services. The
disruption of routine care in 2020, followed by catch-up diagnosis
thereafter,[@vargas-fernandezImpactCOVID19Unmet2025] could have shaped
the apparent timing of the increase independently of any change in true
incidence.

A sustained increase of incidence implies a growing future prevalence of
diabetes and a rising burden of complications and costs, with the
increase among younger adults extending the horizon over which these
consequences will accrue. Our findings reinforce the need for primary
prevention focused on obesity, diet and physical activity, for earlier
detection within primary care, and for strengthened national
surveillance of diabetes and its risk factors.
[@bakNationalDiabetesRegistries2021
@khuntiDiabetesRegistriesHighquality2023] Because our estimates were
produced entirely from routinely collected survey data, the
illness-death approach offers a low-cost, reproducible tool for
monitoring diabetes incidence in Peru and in other countries that lack
diabetes registries or cohorts.

The main strength of this study is the use of nationally representative
survey data covering urban and rural populations across the full
national territory, combined with an established modelling framework
previously validated for chronic conditions.
[@brinksAgeTimedependentModel2014
@silverman-retanaUsingIllnessdeathModel2024] The approach yields
internally consistent age-, sex- and time-specific estimates from
cross-sectional data and avoids the cost and attrition of cohort
studies. Nevertheless, some limitations should be considered. First,
diabetes was defined by self-report of a prior physician diagnosis. This
approach has high specificity but limited sensitivity and does not
capture undiagnosed disease. The IDF estimates that more than four in
ten adults with diabetes are unaware of their
condition.[@maglianoDiabetesAtlas2025] Our incidence estimates therefore
reflect diagnosed diabetes and are conservative relative to total
(diagnosed plus undiagnosed) incidence. They also partly reflect
diagnostic activity and access to care, which changed over the study
period. Second, the data do not distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes,
although the great majority of adult-onset cases are type 2; the rising
incidence of type 1 diabetes reported globally is a further reason for
caution.[@gregoryGlobalIncidencePrevalence2022] Third, no Peruvian
estimate of the diabetes-related MRR was available, therefore we rely on
data from the National Danish Diabetes
Register.[@carstensenPrevalenceIncidenceMortality2020] Based on an
argument from Breslow & Day, the MRR is stable across different
populations.[@statisticalmethodsincancerresearch]

In conclusion, this study provides national, age- and sex-specific
estimates of diabetes incidence in Peru, showing an approximate doubling
between 2016 and 2023. Obtained from routine survey data through the
illness-death model, these findings support strengthened prevention and
surveillance and demonstrate a transferable approach for settings
without diabetes cohorts.

## Table 2. Age-standardized incidence rates of diabetes for men and women in Peru for the years 2016-2023, and the temporal change in incidence rates between 2015 and 2023

```{r Table 2, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,error=FALSE}
inc_standardized <- readRDS(file = here::here("Data/inc.standardized.rds"))

inc_standardized_tbl <- inc_standardized |> 
  mutate(
    Sex = factor(Sex, levels = c("Men", "Women")),
    Year = as.factor(Year),

    # Scale incidence to per 1,000 PY
    inc = inc * 1000,
    inc.lcl = inc.lcl * 1000,
    inc.ucl = inc.ucl * 1000
  )

inc_standardized_tbl <- inc_standardized_tbl  |> 
  mutate(
    `IR (95% CI)` =
      sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", inc, inc.lcl, inc.ucl),

    `IRR (95% CI)` =
      sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", IRR, IRR.lcl, IRR.ucl)
  ) |> 
  select(Sex, Year,
         `IR (95% CI)`,
         `IRR (95% CI)`)

inc_wide <- inc_standardized_tbl  |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Sex,
    values_from = c(`IR (95% CI)`, `IRR (95% CI)`),
    names_glue = "{Sex} – {.value}"
  ) |> 
  relocate("Women – IR (95% CI)",.after = "Men – IRR (95% CI)")

inc_wide_ft <- inc_wide |>
  flextable() |>
  add_header_row(
    values = c("", "Men", "", "Women", ""),
    colwidths = c(1,1,1,1,1)
  ) |>
  set_header_labels(
    Year = "Year",
    `Men – IR (95% CI)` = "IR (95% CI)",
    `Men – IRR (95% CI)` = "IRR (95% CI)",
    `Women – IR (95% CI)` = "IR (95% CI)",
    `Women – IRR (95% CI)` = "IRR (95% CI)"
  ) |>
      padding(padding = 2, part = "all") |>

  autofit() |> 
align(align = "center", part = "all")

inc_wide_ft
```

## Table 3. Age and sex-specific incidence rates of diabetes in Peru for the years 2016-2023, and the temporal change in incidence rates between 2016 and 2023

```{r Table 3, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,error=FALSE}

# Read the data
inc_agespecific <- readRDS(file = here::here("Data/inc.agespecific.rds"))

#Process the data
inc_agespecific_tbl <- inc_agespecific |> 
  mutate(
    Sex = factor(Sex, levels = c("Men", "Women")),
    Year = as.factor(Year),
    age = as.factor(age),
    # Scale incidence to per 1,000 PY
    inc = inc * 1000,
    inc.lcl = inc.lcl * 1000,
    inc.ucl = inc.ucl * 1000
  )

#Format incidence rates and IRRs
inc_agespecific_tbl <- inc_agespecific_tbl  |> 
  mutate(
    `IR (95% CI)` =
      sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", inc, inc.lcl, inc.ucl),

    `IRR (95% CI)` =
      if_else(
        IRR == 1 & IRR.lcl == 1 & IRR.ucl == 1,
        "1.00 (REF)",
        sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", IRR, IRR.lcl, IRR.ucl)
      )
  ) |> 
  select(Sex, age, Year,
         `IR (95% CI)`,
         `IRR (95% CI)`)

#Reshape to  wide format
inc_agespecific_wide <- inc_agespecific_tbl  |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Sex,
    values_from = c(`IR (95% CI)`, `IRR (95% CI)`),
    names_glue = "{Sex} – {.value}"
  )

#order columns
inc_agespecific_wide <- inc_agespecific_wide |> 
  relocate(Year, age,
           "Men – IR (95% CI)",
           "Men – IRR (95% CI)",
           "Women – IR (95% CI)",
           "Women – IRR (95% CI)")

# Convert to flextable
inc_agespecific_wide_ft <- inc_agespecific_wide  |> 
  flextable() |>
  add_header_row(
    values = c("","", "Men", "", "Women", ""),
    colwidths = c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
  ) |>
  set_header_labels(
    age = "Age",
    Year = "Year",
    `Men – IR (95% CI)` = "IR (95% CI)",
    `Men – IRR (95% CI)` = "IRR (95% CI)",
    `Women – IR (95% CI)` = "IR (95% CI)",
    `Women – IRR (95% CI)` = "IRR (95% CI)"
  ) |>
    padding(
      padding = 2,
      part = "all") |>
    autofit() |> 
  align(
    align = "center",
    part = "all")

inc_agespecific_wide_ft
```
